I'm referring to the first of the two documents that you used, Mr. Elderkin, with the witness on recross [sic]. The B/C/S version of which carries ERN number 0431-7318. Could you kindly give us the corresponding English ERN? It's the same one? All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just clarify...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come to the second in due course. So this one, we are referring only for the time being to document with ERN 0431-7318. Any objections from any of the Defence teams? We hear none. Now we come to the other document that the Prosecution made use of with the witness on recross [sic]. The B/C/S and the English text have the same ERN, and that is 0425-4341 to 342. Mr. Petrusic, could you specify your objection, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll act in accordance with your suggestion. The essence of my objection was that the signature that this document bears is not Radivoje Miletic's signature, but the Defence in no way contests the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the document is admitted, unless there is some other objection from the Defence. Of course the question of the authenticity of the signature that appears on the same document remains unprejudiced, is not prejudiced in other words, by the fact that the document is admitted. All right. Mr. Josse -- I take it there are no further documents that you wish to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No further documents, Mr. President, simply a clarification on the second document which I should probably have said a couple of minutes before, but that it was approved for the 65 ter list by the 6th of December decision, if that's a useful orientation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's better. Thank you. Three documents are admitted, yeah. And none will be under seal because we did not actually issue protective measures. So they will remain. Mr. Josse, you have distributed a list. I'll see whether we can dispense of having to go through it. It has been circulated. Mr. Elderkin, I'll start with you. Do you have any objections to the admission of any of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: We don't, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Any of the other Defence teams wish to object to the admission of any of these documents? None. So they are all admitted, unless you wish to state anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is something I would like to state if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That relates to the issue I alluded to at the beginning of today's session. Because now might be a convenient time to deal with this. As I have already stated, there were quite a large number of documents that go to the issue of weapons being received in the enclave, in fact it relates to both enclaves, for what it's worth. And the Prosecution have agreed, as I understand it, that these can be introduced as a batch in order to save, as I have already said, significant time in putting them to any given witness. I should know, there are about 18 documents in total. We provided the Prosecution and all my learned friends not just with the documents, but also with a schedule which I could hand to the Court. I am not asking the schedule itself be admitted as an exhibit. However, it might prove a useful aide-memoire to the Chamber, but it has no evidential significance whatsoever. Let me make that clear. I've been asked to do that by the Prosecution and I'm happy to do that. If we could proceed in that way, I would be very grateful. The schedule also contains the proposed exhibit numbers and probably little more need be said other than that they then be admitted, subject to the view of Your Honours, of course, into the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. Mr. Elderkin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Insofar as the admission of the documents, as we have indicated to my learned friend, then we have no objection. We would have no objection if he had chosen to use those documents with the witness, but we fully appreciate that the time saving is a great grace. To the extent that it's our position that these are concerning the agreed fact of the transportation of arms into the enclave and the helicopters were breaching -- Muslim helicopters were breaching the no-fly zone, we don't see this goes to a contested matter, but in terms of the schedule we don't object to that. We would consider it to be a somewhat adversarial document insofar as it highlights what Defence considers important in those documents, but we don't object to it being included in the way that was suggested. Sorry, adjudicated facts, not agreed facts. If I could make the right reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you very much, Mr. Elderkin. Are your colleagues also familiar with this list and schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They have been sent the schedule. I have informed them orally of what I have agreed with Mr. Elderkin. I hope they are all in agreement. I apologise to them if I've put anyone in an awkward position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am pointing this out because at the back of our minds there is always this possibility that with seven accused you can come to a point where there is evidence which creates a conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect I agree entirely with Your Honour and indeed I mean those issues as to whether defendants are entitled to have bilateral agreements with the Prosecution. I certainly don't want to go there at the moment. That's a difficult jurisprudential issue or perhaps practical issue as well. I think we are all in agreement that these documents can be introduced. Could I hand out the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Madam Usher, could you assist him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As I have already said, I regard this as no more than a working document and if at any stage any of the advocates in this case wish to make some corrections or additions, then that would be quite understandable, and subject to those additions or amendments being on the face of the document, of course we would agree to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's do it in two stages. I will start first with the first list that you distributed, to which I hear no objection, neither from the Prosecution nor from the other Defence teams. Since we are talking of a considerable number of documents now, I think I will just mention the 65 ter number: 6D39, 6D47, 6D49, 6D51, 6D69, 6D71, 6D72, 6D73, 6D77, 6D78, 6D81, 6D82, 6D97. Have -- all these seem to have been translation except one, and that is 6D78. So for the time being, that will be marked for identification, until translation thereof is made available. Now we come to the second batch of exhibits. The understanding is this: At present I am not hearing any objections, either from the Prosecution or from any of the other Defence teams, but I will give one day's grace to members of the Defence teams if any one of you wish to make submissions in relation to the admissibility of any of these documents that I am now going to mention. They are all being admitted with this caveat. 6D52, 6D53, 6D96, 5D7, 6D55, 6D56, 6D57, 6D58, 6D59, 6D60, 6D61, 6D62, 6D63, 6D64, 6D65, 6D66, 6D67, 6D95, and that's the end. I am not in a position to know whether all these have been translated into English. If any of them haven't, then they will be marked for identification. You need to identify any that have not yet been translated, Madam Registrar, and they will be marked for identification pending translation thereof. All others will be admitted with the caveat I mentioned a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Perhaps we could go into private session for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We come to the -- I see you still standing, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Partly out of a matter of courtesy, but also simply to say, to thank the Chamber and all my learned friends for their cooperation in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we thank you in turn, Mr. Josse. The Miletic Defence team, I understand you have several documents you wish to tender, you have also distributed a list. So I will try and adopt the same procedures, sparing us having to go through it in detail. Is there any objection to the admission of any of these documents on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On part of any of the other Defence teams? We hear none. So I am just going to mention the 65 ter number and then state which ones will remain marked for identification for the time being. 5D223, 5D237, 5D233, 5D218, 5D225, 5D235, 5D229, 5D227, 5D259, 5D241 and 5D244. Of these, only 5D237, 5D233, 5D241 will -- are admitted immediately. The others will remain marked for identification pending the translation thereof. And that concludes this witness. Now, before -- yes, I saw you standing, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was just going to switch places with Mr. Elderkin for the next witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will soon be admitting in the courtroom Witness number 49, for whom the Prosecution have sought three protective measures. Correct me if I'm wrong. Pseudonym, facial distortion, and also voice distortion in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That has been objected to by the Defence of General Gvero. Yesterday, in speaking on the protective measures for this witness we've just finished, Mr. Josse also stated a few things in relation to this next witness. As we did yesterday, we are inviting you now to tell us which issues or which questions you would like us to address to the witness. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly the same. The submissions I made yesterday really apply to both of these witnesses. The issue as to whether there is any possibility of the witness accepting facial and voice distortion but not pseudonym is particularly pertinent to him, in our submission. Other than that, if I may, Your Honour, with respect, ask the questions yesterday that we would have asked, had we been in the position to do so, and there is nothing more I can add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I think I will take on board Judge Kwon's suggestion at this time and have the break now. All right. So Madam Usher, could -- we'll interview him in private session as we did with the previous one. So -- or in closed session, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I know that so far as this witness is concerned, I will have a short submission to make after the Court has heard the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We have received Mr. Beara's waiver. The other thing I wanted to inform you about is that, as we told you we would be doing, we wrote to the President in the wake of the statement that we made a few days back in relation to Ms. Condon's submission, and he has sent us a reply, we just wanted to confirm that to you. Now, I don't think it's the case of interviewing this witness any further. We'd like to hear any submissions that you may have. Or else hear what I might propose on behalf of the -- because we've been discussing obviously, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, as a possible formula. We had in mind suggesting the granting only of facial distortion and nothing else, and then perhaps, as we did yesterday, we would try to avoid referring to the witness by name.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have already indicated, on behalf of our client, that we have no objection to facial distortion only. So far as not referring to him by name is concerned, whilst in terms of actually asking questions, that is possible and indeed speaking again on behalf of myself, I am more than happy to do that when I come to cross-examine him. Practically, it is going to be very difficult for his name not to become apparent from his evidence. Could we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session for a short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would anyone else wish to make a statement or remark or comment on what I stated? Yes, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we may move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, I'm going explain to the public the result of our decision, because frankly, I think we could have been in open session while we were doing that. The result is that we are not granting all the provisional -- the protective measures that have been requested by the Prosecution. We are only granting face distortion, and for -- granting face distortion and that's it. So we can proceed along those lines. Thank you. Mr. Thayer. Perhaps for your first questions we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Sir, when you arrived in Zepa in 1993, what sort of civilian authority existed there then?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since before the war Zepa was just a local commune in the municipality of Rogatica, there were practically no civilian authorities, at least not at a high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: So was some sort of civilian authority established during the war, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up until my arrival I believe there was a War Presidency, I don't know all the details. But there were no other organised forms of power, given all the events this wasn't something that anyone worked on that's up until my arrival in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Okay. Without at this point mentioning any particular names, can you please describe for the Trial Chamber, after your arrival in Zepa, how was this War Presidency further established or refined? And what were its functions, if you could just describe for the Court in basic terms, sir.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, immediately after my arrival in Zepa the Republika Srpska army launched an attack. That was in the spring of 1993. And on that occasion the first protected areas were established in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Zepa was one such area. In the spring of 1993 there was a Security Council resolution which established Zepa as a protected zone, or as one of the protected zones. UNPROFOR forces arrived in Zepa, Zepa was demilitarised, and during that period of time the War Presidency was also established. The first president of the War Presidency, who had also held that position up until that point in time, suggested that I be the president of the Executive Board, and at the same time a member of the War Presidency. The position I held was, in fact, a position that involved organising civilian life in the territory of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I -- I was hoping to avoid this. I was -- wanted to go into private session for the last subject matter. If I could just ask for redaction and move into private session. The portion at line 70 -- I'm sorry, page 70, line 25, through page 71, line 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why are you seeking that redaction?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Because it specifically identifies the position he occupied, and I think we can navigate around that through the further examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you had finished. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, I had, Your Honour. It's -- I had. I mean I think we can -- we can refer to his position and so forth as a way of mitigating the exposure, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's going to be extremely difficult, and in our submission it runs contrary to the decision the Chamber made earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We made our position clear earlier on, Mr. Thayer, that we are not granting the use of a pseudonym. And that's because we are not convinced that there is justification for the granting of that protective measure. Only concession that we have made about, apart from the face distortion, is based on the agreement with the various Defence teams that we try not to use his name. But basically, I mean, it would be running contrary and would defeat the whole purpose of our decision if we were even to suppress information on who -- what position he occupied, what role he played. The whole purpose was to be in open session as much as possible. This gentleman occupied a certain position during the conflict. His evidence is necessary, is required, because you have summoned him. But that's about it. I mean we have hidden his face to make him feel more at ease when he travels around -- around in Bosnia, because many people may be following his testimony. Some would know who he is, even if we redact this and redact others. Some people would definitely identify him, but many won't, and still many others won't, because they won't see his face. Okay? So let's leave it at that. No redactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I appreciate the Court's consideration on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Sir, can you continue to explain to the Trial Chamber the basic functions that the War Presidency served the Zepa enclave during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can say that three of the main functions that I was to perform, as the president of the Executive Board, are as follows: Firstly, there was the organisation of the distribution of humanitarian aid. I'm referring to the aid that arrived through the UNHCR. And, as far as I can remember, it arrived from Belgrade for the eastern enclaves. Secondly, my function was to organise the work of hospitals, of medical care. And thirdly, a very important function that I had was to attempt to organise the primary school, which, up until the beginning of the war, was there in the area. I was involved in those activities. We established other organisational units in order to carry out all these activities. The civilian police was then organised in an appropriate manner. And as of May 1993, until, roughly speaking, mid-1995, civilian life in Zepa was, on the whole, made normal. And for the inhabitants of the area, it was more or less possible for them to live there. It was bearable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Sir, you just referred to the civilian police. Was there somebody who was in charge of that, and what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer that question and provide the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hurem Sahic was the chief of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Was there also a civilian protection organisation that was set up?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I failed to mention this fact because that wasn't my responsibility, so to speak. There was a civilian protection force that had been organised, and I think it was at the end of 1992. It was one of the first groups to be organised, and it was also responsible for assisting the inhabitants. And later for constructing accommodation, because there were a lot of refugees in Zepa, there were far more who had arrived there than there were people who actually had houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: What was the name of person that headed up the civilian protection organisation?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Amir Imamovic is his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And did the War Presidency have a president, sir? And, if so, what was that person's name?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The War Presidency did have a president. He was also the president of the Zepa municipality later on, because during a period of time the authorities in Sarajevo recognised Zepa as a municipality. When I was selected as president of the Executive Board, the president of the Presidency was Mr. Benjamin Kulovac. And later there were two replacements, but in May 1993 the president of the War Presidency was Mr. Benjamin Kulovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And how about in 1995, sir, who was the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time the president of the War Presidency was Mr. Mehmed Hajric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And briefly, sir, could you describe what the duties and responsibilities of the president of the War Presidency were at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can remember, whenever he had contact with international organisations, UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, military observers, Doctors Without Borders, since I think that they had their own mission in Zepa for a certain period of time, whenever he had contact with those organisations, he was to represent Zepa and agree on various forms of assistance and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And Mr. Hajric, do you recall what his occupation was, independent of being the president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a religious cleric, that was his profession. He was a Hodja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And occasionally I've seen that position of president of the War Presidency referred to as the mayor of Zepa. Is that a fair way to describe the president of the War Presidency, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. Because that's how all the foreigners who were there referred to that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, in 1993, a census was conducted in Zepa. Can you tell the Trial Chamber why that was done, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the military activities came to an end in a certain extent, and humanitarian aid had been organised, it was essential to carry out a census of the population in order to have a plan for the distribution of the humanitarian aid, whenever it was to be delivered. So the census was carried out in the villages and by visiting families.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And approximately how many people did the census conclude lived in the Zepa enclave, sir, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the first census was taken -- when the first census was taken there were between eight and 9.000 inhabitants. But later, due to migration, the figure in 1995 was about 7.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Now, you've referred already to the declaration of Zepa as a safe area, and the presence of UNPROFOR soldiers. Did you become acquainted with their commander, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Ukrainian Battalion was present in Zepa. The commander of the UNPROFOR mission in Zepa was Colonel Semjon Dudnik. We did meet, I think he was there at the beginning in 1993. And to a certain extent we cooperated right up until the end of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how many soldiers Colonel Dudnik commanded there in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the number may have varied, but, in fact, we didn't have any information on the number, on their strength, but given the way in which they were organised, given the way in which the UNPROFOR mission in Zepa had been organised, well my assessment would be that there were about 80 soldiers and officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: And just in the short time we have left, sir, can you describe for the Trial Chamber how those soldiers were deployed, physically, in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MEHO DZEBO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR forces in Zepa were based in the primary school in the very centre of Zepa. There were check-points that had been set up at all routes of access to the Zepa enclave. And, as far as I can remember, there was one armoured vehicle at each check-point, and a permanent UNPROFOR presence. In this case they were Ukrainian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. I think we have to stop here for the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Madam Usher will escort you out of the courtroom. And before you leave, sir, between today and tomorrow, when we hope to finish with your testimony, if we can, it's important that you do not communicate or allow anyone to communicate with you to discuss the subject matter of your testimony. It's very important. Thank you. May I also invite the Defence teams to come back with a response tomorrow morning in relation to the protective measures asked for Witness 135, please. Okay. Thank you. Have a nice evening, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 30th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
